--- title: "Simulation Based Estimation of Sampling Bias" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 bibliography: ../paper/references.bib --- ```{=html} ``` # Data and models **Field.** GLORYS12V1 reanalysis on its native $1/12^\circ$ grid. OHC is the $0$–$2000$ m depth integral of potential temperature against constant $c_p\rho$ (`code/ohc.py`), evaluated daily over 2010–2019. Cells enter the analysis only where $\mathrm{deptho} > 2000$ m *and* the integral is defined at every level. **Mean field.** OHC is split as $\mathrm{OHC} = \hat m + \tilde Z$ into a smooth climatological mean field $\hat m$, fitted once across $1995$–$2019$, and the residual anomaly field $\tilde Z$. $\hat m$ is a per-cell OLS on a quadratic trend plus annual and semiannual harmonics, fit against the GLORYS *monthly* record with each basis function averaged over its month to match the monthly-mean response, then evaluated pointwise per day. @sec-meanfield gives the estimator and summarizes what it leaves. **Advection.** OceanParcels, park depth $1000$ m, advected by GLORYS daily $(u,v)$ over $11$–$66^\circ$ N, $87$–$12^\circ$ W -- the full 2010-2019 footprint of every float that profiles an analysis box in 2015-2019, so simulated floats are not deleted for leaving the velocity domain (an earlier $15$–$50^\circ$ N, $70$–$30^\circ$ W domain lost most such floats at its western edge; see @sec-retention). Floats advect continuously at park depth and record a position every $10$ days; there is no ascent, descent or surface drift, so a cycle is a position sample, not a simulated dive. Floats are deleted on leaving the velocity domain and retired at a lifespan drawn from the real Argo record for this region (median $\approx 1500$ d). **Estimation.** $\hat Z_k$ is the unweighted mean of $\tilde Z_k$ at the profile positions for year $k$, and $\bar Z_k$ is the exact $\mathbb{P}$-weighted domain mean of the same field for year $k$. # The analysis domain Two analysis boxes sit inside the downloaded GLORYS region, both spanning $60^\circ$–$40^\circ$ W: **Box B** ($34$–$45^\circ$ N) straddles the North Atlantic Current and the Gulf Stream extension, and **Box A** ($22$–$34^\circ$ N) has milder currents and OHC variability. The boxes are **contiguous** at $34^\circ$ N, so their union is a connected domain and $A\cup B$ is itself a well-defined estimand; the boundary row belongs to Box B, which is why Box A's stated upper bound is a fraction below $34^\circ$ (the bounds are inclusive and the native grid has a row exactly there, which would otherwise fall in both boxes and be counted twice in the union). The OHC field is built over a **conditioning buffer** ($14$–$55^\circ$ N, $72$–$32^\circ$ W), roughly ten degrees beyond the boxes on every side. Kriging a point near a box edge needs profiles from outside that box, so the buffer, not the box, sets how far the field must extend; velocity was downloaded over a larger region still, and floats are lost if they leave it. ::: {#cell-fig-domain .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The two analysis boxes (filled) inside the downloaded GLORYS velocity and thetao regions (dashed).](osim_files/figure-html/fig-domain-output-1.png){#fig-domain width=837 height=622} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-bathy .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![GLORYS ocean depth over the advection domain (left) and the sub-2000 m cells excluded from the analysis (right), both boxes outlined.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-bathy-output-1.png){#fig-bathy width=1402 height=564} ::: ::: An analysis mask is placed on cells that must have temperature data for every depth level to $2000$m. Retained area is $92.35\%$ and $99.77\%$ for Box B and A respectively. The below figures show a single day's OHC anomaly and velocity fields for the analysis domain. A day was selected based on its percentile of spatial variability across cells for the given field over both analysis boxes. ::: {#cell-fig-days .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Residual field Z (GJ per m2) on days at the 5th, 50th and 95th percentile of the combined daily spatial dispersion, both boxes on one shared diverging scale.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-days-output-1.png){#fig-days width=1403 height=535} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-vel-u .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Eastward velocity at 1000 m (cm/s), both boxes on one shared diverging scale.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-vel-u-output-1.png){#fig-vel-u width=1403 height=535} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-vel-v .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Northward velocity at 1000 m (cm/s), both boxes on one shared diverging scale.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-vel-v-output-1.png){#fig-vel-v width=1403 height=544} ::: ::: **The flow is roughly twice as variable in Box B.** Median daily $\mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}$ is $12.1$ cm/s eastward and $11.5$ northward in Box B against $5.5$ and $5.4$ in Box A. Over 2010-2019, the range of daily spatial standard deviation in cm/s is $9.7$–$14.8$ (eastward) and $9.0$–$14.7$ (northward) in Box B, $4.5$–$7.0$ (eastward) and $4.4$–$6.7$ (northward) in Box A. # Mean field {#sec-meanfield} The sampling-bias question concerns the *residual anomaly* OHC field, not the total. We therefore decompose $$\mathrm{OHC}(c,t) \;=\; \hat m(c,t) \;+\; \tilde Z(c,t),$$ with $\hat m$ a mean field fitted per cell once across all years and $\tilde Z_k$ the year-$k$ residual the designs sample. **Regression.** For each analysis cell $c$, OHC is modelled as $\mathrm{OHC}(c,t) = \phi(t)^\top \beta_c + \varepsilon(c,t)$ on the trend-plus-harmonics basis $\phi(t) = \bigl(1,\,t,\,t^2,\,\sin 2\pi t,\,\cos 2\pi t,\,\sin 4\pi t,\,\cos 4\pi t\bigr)^\top$ ($t$ in decimal years): a quadratic trend and the annual and semiannual cycles. The coefficients are fit by least squares to the $1995$–$2019$ GLORYS *monthly* mean record. A GLORYS monthly file holds the month *mean* OHC over $I_m = [t_0^m, t_1^m)$ but is time-stamped at its start $t_0^m$. So we regress on the **window-averaged basis** $\bar\phi(I_m) = |I_m|^{-1}\!\int_{I_m}\phi(t)\,dt$, so the OHC monthly response and seasonal basis are monthly averages. The design matrix is $\bar X = \bigl[\bar\phi(I_m)^\top\bigr]_m$ and the per-cell fit is $\hat\beta_c = \bar X^{+} Y_c$. **Prediction is then pointwise:** the fitted field is evaluated at each instant on the daily grid, $\hat m(c,t) = \phi(t)^\top \hat\beta_c$, and subtracted from daily OHC to give $\tilde Z_k = \mathrm{OHC}_k - \hat m$ on the same mask. ::: {#cell-fig-meanfield .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Fitted mean field (quadratic trend plus annual and semiannual harmonics) at mid-month 2015, both boxes on one shared scale, in GJ per m2.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-meanfield-output-1.png){#fig-meanfield width=1484 height=475} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-decomp3 .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The OHC = mean field + residual decomposition on one shared day, both boxes drawn per field, in GJ per m2.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-decomp3-output-1.png){#fig-decomp3 width=1469 height=681} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ohc-series .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Daily domain-mean OHC with the fitted mean field (top) and their difference, the domain-mean anomaly (bottom), per box over 2010-2019 in GJ per m2.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-ohc-series-output-1.png){#fig-ohc-series width=1199 height=704} ::: ::: # Estimand, truth, and estimator Let $\mathbb{P}$ be the normalized area $\times$ time probability measure over the depth masked analysis domain. The target is the residual field's domain mean, $$\bar Z_k \;=\; \int_{\mathcal{X}} \tilde Z_k \, d\mathbb{P},$$ for each analysis year $k$, where $\tilde Z_k$ is the year-$k$ OHC 0–2000 m field with the fitted mean field removed. A design is a finite point set $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n} \subset \mathcal{X}$ — the year-$k$ in-box profiles of one deployment realization $d$; its estimator and bias are $$\hat Z^{(d)}_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tilde Z_k\!\left(x_i^{(d)}\right), \qquad B^{(d)}_k \;=\; \hat Z^{(d)}_k - \bar Z_k .$$ $\tilde Z_k$ is a simple function on the native $1/12^\circ \times$ daily grid, so evaluating it at $x_i$ is the cell-day lookup of the *containing* cell. **A class of linear estimators.** Both estimators reported here are linear in the field, $\hat Z = \sum_i a_i \tilde Z(x_i)$, so each carries a signed *estimator measure* $\mathbb{Q} = \sum_i a_i \delta_{x_i}$ and the bias is an inner product, $B = \langle \tilde Z, \mathbb{Q} - \mathbb{P}\rangle$. Writing $m = \mathbb{E}\big[\sum_i a_i\big]$ for the expected total mass, the design-averaged bias splits as $$\mathbb{E}[B] \;=\; \underbrace{\int_{\mathcal{X}} \big(\tilde Z_k - \bar Z_k\big)\, d\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{Q}]}_{\text{alignment}} \;+\; \underbrace{(m-1)\,\bar Z_k}_{\text{coverage}} .$$ The alignment term measures how far the expected sampling weight correlates with the field; the coverage term is a pure shrinkage, proportional to the estimand, that appears only when the estimator fails to conserve mass. The identity is stated density-free because $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{Q}]$ need not be absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathbb{P}$ — the kriging estimator draws on profiles outside the box and outside year $k$ — and reduces to $\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb{P}}(w, \tilde Z_k) + (m-1)\bar Z_k$ with $w = d\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{Q}]/d\mathbb{P}$ whenever that density exists. *Simple mean.* $a_i = 1/n$, so $\sum_i a_i = 1$ for every realization: $m \equiv 1$, the coverage term vanishes identically, and the whole bias is alignment. *Simple kriging.* Predict on a $1^\circ \times 1^\circ \times$ month grid and average with area-time weights $c_g$ summing to one, giving $a_i = \sum_g c_g\,\alpha_i(x^*_g)$ with $\alpha_i(x^*)$ the kriging weights. Simple kriging reverts to its zero prior mean where under-informed, so $\sum_i a_i \le 1$ and the coverage term is live. @sec-krige gives the covariance model. ::: {#2abd3fe5 .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

The dispersion $\sigma_k = \mathrm{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z_k)$ is $6.3$–$7.6$ GJ/m$^2$ in Box B and $1.7$–$2.4$ in Box A. # Deployment One continuous advection per realization generates the sampling. For realization $d$, $N$ floats are seeded uniformly over normalized spacetime across the velocity record of 2010-2019. Each realization therefore yields $B^{(d)}_k$ for every analysis year at once, flow and field the same calendar year. **How a float is advected.** Each float is carried by GLORYS12V1 daily horizontal velocity $(u,v)$ at a fixed park depth of $1000$ m and held there for its whole life — there is *no dive cycle*. The two archived velocity levels bracketing $1000$ m ($902$ and $1062$ m) are linearly interpolated to the park depth (as OceanParcels does natively), and the float is stepped forward at a $1$-hour time step. Its position is written every $10$ days, and that recorded park-depth position is taken as the profile — the point where a real float would begin its ascent — so a cycle is a position sample, not a simulated dive. A float is deleted when it leaves the velocity domain and retired at a lifespan drawn from the real Argo record (median $\approx 1500$ d). The ensemble is **$50$ independent realizations**. Each seeds **$1{,}000$ floats** uniformly over normalized space–time on the ($\mathrm{deptho}\ge 1000$ m) part of $11$–$63^\circ$ N, $80$–$24^\circ$ W — the conditioning buffer plus an $8^\circ$ advective margin, capped by the velocity domain — across $2010\text{-}01\text{-}01$ to $2019\text{-}12\text{-}26$, and advects them once at $1000$ m park depth ($10$-day profiling cycle, lifespans drawn from the real Argo record). Years $2010$–$2014$ are the equilibration lead; bias is calculated on **$2015$–$2019$**. Seeding follows the region the analysis *reads out*, not the estimand: an array seeded only around the boxes leaves the buffer edge populated by advective inflow alone, a coverage deficit that is an artifact of the seeding rectangle rather than of the observing system. Widening the seed region to $1.86\times$ its previous area at a fixed float count also brings the in-box standing stock down close to the real Argo density (below), which matters because an over-dense array inflates $m$ and would understate the coverage term. **Every profile is recorded**, in or out of a box, with its exact timestamp — about $3.3\times$ as many rows as the in-box subset. Only in-box profiles enter the simple-mean estimate, but the kriging estimator conditions on profiles from the whole buffer, and keeping the full footprint means the analysis region can be changed later without re-advecting. ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Simulated advection ::: {#cell-fig-advection .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![One simulated deployment: 60 float drift tracks and their 10-day profile points coloured by year, only in-box profiles (filled) entering an estimate.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-advection-output-1.png){#fig-advection width=947 height=648} ::: ::: ### Real Argo ::: {#cell-fig-advection-argo .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Real Argo trajectories over the same domain and years (60 of 740 floats) coloured by year, on the same base map for comparison.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-advection-argo-output-1.png){#fig-advection-argo width=947 height=648} ::: ::: ::: **Real deployment geometry.** The map below shows the raw (not QC-cleaned) deployment position of every real Argo float first observed inside the advection domain over $2010$–$2019$ ($1{,}014$ floats), coloured by deployment year — the release geometry the real-deployment arms (below) seed from, and the starting point for the per-float bias-over-time analysis. Deployment is taken as each float's earliest profile on record, so a float first observed before the file window is not resolved here. ::: {#cell-fig-deploy-positions .cell execution_count=13} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Raw Argo deployment positions in the advection domain, 2010-2019, coloured by deployment year, on the shared domain base map (dashed: velocity and thetao download regions; filled: the two analysis boxes).](osim_files/figure-html/fig-deploy-positions-output-1.png){#fig-deploy-positions width=947 height=648} ::: ::: ## A single deployment cluster {#sec-cluster} Six floats were deployed within a $\sim\!14$-hour window on $27$–$28$ September $2015$ in a tight cluster in the NW corner of Box B ($43.4$–$44.3^\circ$ N, $-55.8$ to $-57.8^\circ$ W), on the Grand Banks / Gulf Stream–Labrador confluence. They are a clean natural experiment in deployment geometry: a common release point and time, whose per-float sampling bias we can then follow profile by profile. For the simple-mean estimator the year-$k$ bias is an *exact* sum of per-profile contributions. Writing $n_k$ for the number of in-box profiles the array reports in year $k$, $$ B_k \;=\; \hat Z_k - \bar Z_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\bigl(\tilde Z_k(x_i) - \bar Z_k\bigr) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n_k} c_i, \qquad c_i \;=\; \frac{1}{n_k}\,\underbrace{\bigl(\tilde Z_k(x_i) - \bar Z_k\bigr)}_{\delta_i}, $$ the centering being free because $\tfrac{1}{n_k}\sum_i \bar Z_k = \bar Z_k$. Every profile carries the *same* weight $1/n_k$ whatever float it came from — that equal weighting is what makes the estimator the simple (unweighted) mean, and it ties the normalization to the year, not the float. Grouping the contributions by float gives each float's share of the year's bias, $$ C_{f,k} \;=\; \sum_{i\,\in\, f,\,k} c_i \;=\; \frac{n_{f,k}}{n_k}\bigl(\bar Z_{f,k} - \bar Z_k\bigr), \qquad \sum_f C_{f,k} = B_k, $$ its profile share $n_{f,k}/n_k$ times its mean alignment $\bar Z_{f,k} - \bar Z_k$ (with $\bar Z_{f,k}$ the mean of $\tilde Z_k$ over that float's year-$k$ in-box profiles). The charts below plot the single-profile bias $\delta_i = \tilde Z_k(x_i) - \bar Z_k$ — one profile's alignment with the field — along each float's life (in-box profiles only, where the residual field is defined), with the cluster mean over-plotted. This is the contribution $c_i$ up to the $1/n_k$ weight; we show $\delta_i$ rather than $c_i$ so the curves stay comparable across years (the year's $n_k$ only rescales them). The two tabs evaluate $\delta_i$ at the *real* Argo positions and at the *GLORYS park-advection* sim-twin positions of the same floats, so their divergence is the same real-vs-reanalysis gap the trajectory maps show. ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Real Argo ::: {#cell-fig-cluster-bias .cell execution_count=14} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Single-profile bias Z(x_i) - Zbar_k (GJ per m2) vs profile number for each of the six floats at their real Argo positions, with the cluster mean (black). Only in-box profiles carry a defined bias.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-cluster-bias-output-1.png){#fig-cluster-bias width=1198 height=539} ::: ::: ### GLORYS advection ::: {#cell-fig-cluster-bias-sim .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The same single-profile bias evaluated at the GLORYS 1000 m park-advection sim-twin positions of the six floats. In-box counts differ from the real tab because the park tracks drift out of the box on a different schedule.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-cluster-bias-sim-output-1.png){#fig-cluster-bias-sim width=1198 height=539} ::: ::: ::: The two trajectory maps below trace the same six floats (one colour each; deployment a star, last fix an open circle): the GLORYS park-advection sim twin against the real Argo path from the shared deployment. ::: {.panel-tabset} ### GLORYS advection ::: {#cell-fig-cluster-sim .cell execution_count=16} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![GLORYS 1000 m park-advection sim-twin trajectories of the six floats from their real deployment positions.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-cluster-sim-output-1.png){#fig-cluster-sim width=947 height=727} ::: ::: ### Real Argo ::: {#cell-fig-cluster-real .cell execution_count=17} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Real Argo trajectories of the same six floats on the same base map.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-cluster-real-output-1.png){#fig-cluster-real width=947 height=727} ::: ::: ::: ## Domain retention {#sec-retention} The expanded velocity domain almost eliminates the loss of floats to advection out of bounds. The table and map below classify the fate of every virtual float in the **argo-actual arm** ($365$ floats seeded from real deployments, advected once over $2010$–$2019$ on the new domain): each either leaves the velocity domain early (deleted), retires at its drawn lifespan, or is still alive at the record end. Only **$3.6\%$** ($13/365$) exit the domain, and $12$ of those $13$ leave at the *southern* edge ($\sim\!11^\circ$ N) -- the western edge that flushed floats on the old domain is now deep interior. Almost all exits are at the southern boundary.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-domain-exit-output-1.png){#fig-domain-exit width=947 height=727} ::: ::: # The sampling weight field The bias $B^{(d)}_k = \langle \tilde Z_k,\, w^{(d)} - p\rangle$, the inner product of the residual field with the excess of the empirical sampling weight over the uniform weight p. One realization's sampling is the normalized empirical measure $$w^{(d)} \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \delta_{x_i}$$ on the spacetime domain $\mathcal{X} = \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{T}$. Averaging it over realizations gives $\mathbb{E}[w]$, the normalized occupancy (intensity) measure of the advective array, with $\mathbb{E}[B_k] = \langle \tilde Z_k,\, \mathbb{E}[w] - p\rangle$. We define the spatial marginal sampling weight as $$w^{\mathrm{sp}}_c \;=\; \sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}} w_{c,\tau} \;=\; \frac{\#\{\,i : x_i \in c\,\}}{n},$$ the fraction of a realization's profiles that fall in cell $c$, summed over all days. The maps below show $\mathbb{E}[w^{\mathrm{sp}}_c]$ — the expected such fraction, i.e. the array's normalized spatial intensity — over the years $2015$–$2019$ on the native $1/12^\circ$ grid, against the uniform area marginal $p^{\mathrm{sp}}_c = A_c / \sum_{c'} A_{c'}$, as the ratio $q_c = \mathbb{E}[w^{\mathrm{sp}}_c] / p^{\mathrm{sp}}_c$ ($=1$ under area-fair sampling). ## Spatial marginal ::: {#cell-fig-wspace .cell execution_count=20} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Over- and under-sampling log2(E[w]/uniform) on the native 1/12 deg grid, both boxes on one map per scored year and one shared scale (red over-sampled, blue under, white uniform).](osim_files/figure-html/fig-wspace-output-1.png){#fig-wspace width=1692 height=417} ::: ::: The per-cell weight distribution about the uniform value of 1, one panel per year: ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Box B ::: {#cell-fig-whist .cell execution_count=21} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box B distribution of the per-cell weight E[w]/uniform over native cells per year, about the uniform value of 1 (red line).](osim_files/figure-html/fig-whist-output-1.png){#fig-whist width=1417 height=318} ::: ::: ### Box A ::: {#cell-fig-whist-a .cell execution_count=22} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box A distribution of the per-cell weight E[w]/uniform, same construction as Box B.](osim_files/figure-html/fig-whist-a-output-1.png){#fig-whist-a width=1417 height=318} ::: ::: ::: ## Bias as a covariance Let $q = w/p$ be the sampling frequency of each cell-day relative to its uniform share — the over/under-sampling factor mapped in @fig-wspace and distributed in @fig-whist, equal to $1$ under uniform sampling and with $\int q\,\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P} = 1$. The bias is the inner product of the field with the sampling excess, $$B_k \;=\; \langle \tilde Z_k,\, q - 1\rangle_{\mathbb{P}} \;=\; \langle \tilde Z_k - \bar Z_k,\, q - 1\rangle_{\mathbb{P}},$$ the second equality because $\langle 1, q-1\rangle_{\mathbb{P}} = 0$ — a spatially uniform field is sampled without bias. Cauchy–Schwarz for this inner product gives the cap $$|B_k| \;\le\; \lVert \tilde Z_k - \bar Z_k\rVert_{\mathbb{P}}\,\lVert q - 1\rVert_{\mathbb{P}} \;=\; \sigma_k \, \operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q),$$ with $\sigma_k = \operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(\tilde Z_k)$ (the residual-field table) and $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q)$ the spread of the over/under-sampling factor (@fig-whist), attained only when $q-1$ is proportional to the field anomaly. **Zero bias does not require uniform sampling** — it requires only that $q - 1$ be orthogonal to $\tilde Z_k$ in $L^2(\mathbb{P})$; a strongly non-uniform array ($\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q) \gg 0$) can still be unbiased for this functional. # Results ## Pilot specification Across the $50$ realizations the ensemble seeds $5\times10^4$ float-deployments; per-box, per-year sample sizes are in the table below. Box B holds a standing stock of $\sim\!32$–$35$ floats ($\sim\!1{,}150$–$1{,}290$ profiles a year) and Box A $\sim\!43$–$48$ ($\sim\!1{,}560$–$1{,}720$). Per unit area the two are nearly identical — about $17$ floats per $10^6$ km$^2$ — which is what area-uniform seeding should give, and is the reason the pooled estimator below carries almost no allocation bias between the boxes. ::: {#611f2132 .cell execution_count=24} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}

Following Kuusela & Stein, it is fitted **locally**: for each centre $(x^*, y^*, \tau^*)$ on the prediction grid, the window $$\widetilde W = [x^*\pm\lambda_G]\times[y^*\pm\lambda_G]\times[t^*\pm\lambda_t], \qquad \lambda_G = 10^\circ,\ \lambda_t = 45\ \text{d},$$ is collected over every year at the same yearday, and within it the year-$i$ anomaly is a zero-mean Gaussian process with an anisotropic exponential covariance $k = \phi_W\exp(-d)$, $d^2 = (\Delta x/\theta_{W,\text{lon}})^2 + (\Delta y/\theta_{W,\text{lat}})^2 + (\Delta t/\theta_{W,t})^2$, plus an i.i.d. nugget $\sigma^2_W$. Years enter as **i.i.d. replicates**, not pooled: the joint log-likelihood is the *sum* of the per-year log-likelihoods, so the covariance is block diagonal by year and no cross-year lag is ever formed. That is what anchors $\theta_{W,t}$ to lags $\le 2\lambda_t$ — a single pooled fit over the same field returns $\theta_t = 154$ d against an empirical $e$-fold near $20$ d, because it can see multi-year separations. Each block is small enough to factor exactly, so no Vecchia approximation enters. The sill is profiled out analytically, $\hat\phi_W = \sum_i z_i^\top K_i^{-1} z_i / \sum_i n_i$, leaving four free parameters; they are found by L-BFGS-B with analytic gradients. Windows are fitted on a $2^\circ$ grid — adjacent windows share about $81\%$ of their footprint, so the parameter field is smooth and each $1^\circ$ prediction point simply takes its containing cell's values, with no interpolation. Per Kuusela the final plug-ins are the **temporal medians** over the twelve monthly windows, so the fitted field varies spatially but not seasonally. Note the weights are invariant to the sill: since $\Sigma = \phi(R + \tau^2 I)$ and $k^* = \phi\,\bar r$, the kriging weights are $a = (R + \tau^2 I)^{-1}\bar r$. Only the ranges and the nugget *ratio* reach $m$, so nothing about $\hat\phi_W$ propagates into the bias. Fitting the covariance to the *complete* GLORYS field rather than to each realization's own profiles makes it an **oracle**: it is fixed across realizations, so the weights $a_i$ depend on design geometry alone, the estimator is genuinely linear, and $\mathbb{E}[B]$ splits into exactly the two terms above with no parameter-estimation term. Refitting per realization would add that third term — the Diggle preferential-estimation effect — and is deferred. ## Fitted parameters ::: {#6686a88e .cell execution_count=34} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34} ```{=html}

The correlation is *flatter than exponential near the origin* and *far steeper in the tail*, so the likelihood stretches the range to limit the initial drop, and pays for it at every larger lag. Localizing reduced this from $\sim\!8\times$ for a single global fit but did not remove it, because it is a mismatch of kernel *shape*, not of stationarity — shrinking $\lambda_G$ does not help either. The mismatch is essentially spatial: locally the *temporal* exponential is excellent, reproducing the empirical correlation to within a few percent out to $30$ d. The nugget goes to zero almost everywhere, for the same reason plus the absence of measurement error in an oracle fit on complete truth. Both push the same way: ranges that are too long make kriging treat distant profiles as more informative than they are, so the weights sum higher, **$m$ is biased up and the coverage term is understated**. The bias reported here is therefore that of a *misspecified* mapper — which is the object of interest, since this is the covariance the deployed estimator uses — and is not the coverage deficit of an optimal one. ## Bias and its decomposition ::: {#3f9ce265 .cell execution_count=38} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=38} ```{=html}

Whether the bias adds depends on the estimator. **Kriging adds exactly.** Its prediction grid is already weighted by area, so splitting $\sum_g c_g \hat Z(x^*_g)$ over the two boxes gives $\hat Z^{A\cup B} = w_A\hat Z^A + w_B\hat Z^B$, and likewise $m^{A\cup B} = w_A m^A + w_B m^B$. The alignment and coverage terms add the same way. **The simple mean does not.** Pooling the profiles weights each box by its *profile count*, not its area, so with $p_A$ the share of profiles falling in $A$, $$B^{A\cup B} \;=\; p_A B^A + p_B B^B \;+\; \underbrace{(p_A - w_A)\big(\bar Z^A_k - \bar Z^B_k\big)}_{\text{allocation}},$$ a between-box version of the same preferential-sampling mechanism, which vanishes only when the array samples the two boxes in proportion to their areas. ::: {#b750a8d7 .cell execution_count=44} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=44} ```{=html}

It is not identically zero: several years are resolved at $2$–$4$ Monte-Carlo standard errors, so the array is weakly preferential in effect, at a magnitude that is a small fraction of the field's own variability. **Strong non-uniform sampling, nearly orthogonal to the field.** The array samples space genuinely non-uniformly (on-mask up to $\sim\!3.6\times$ over-sampling, $\operatorname{sd}_{\mathbb{P}}(q)\approx0.4$; @fig-whist), yet the bias is only $\sim\!1$–$5\%$ of the Cauchy–Schwarz ceiling that non-uniformity permits, i.e. a weight–field correlation $|\rho_k|\approx0.02$. Preferential sampling does not imply preferential bias for this functional — the estimand-level bias is the covariance $\operatorname{Cov}_{\mathbb{P}}(q,\tilde Z_k)$, and the array sits near its null space, not a property of sampling non-uniformity per se. **Both regimes are comparably biased once standardized.** Box B has larger raw bias and spread, but on the $\sigma_k$ scale the energetic western-boundary region is not disproportionately biased relative to the quiescent gyre.
